branch_provenance.syndrome: Subacute Progressive Gastric Outlet Obstruction with Marked Gastric Distension

state.case_summary:
A previously healthy young man presented during a month of religious fasting with a 1-week history of intractable vomiting, postprandial upper abdominal pain, and bloating. He had been compliant with fasting customs, was markedly lean, and reported progressive inability to tolerate oral intake. On examination, he was dehydrated and exhausted. After initial resuscitation, abdominal ultrasonography and plain radiographs showed marked gastric distension. A nasogastric tube was placed for decompression. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta at an acute angle. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal, with no intrinsic luminal lesions.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome
B. Gastric outlet obstruction was considered given the patient’s intractable vomiting and abdominal distension
C. Peptic stricture of the stomach was considered as a cause of outlet narrowing
D. Neoplasm of the stomach was considered because tumors can obstruct gastric outflow
E. Annular pancreas, diabetic gastroparesis, internal hernia, and duodenal bezoar were considered as alternative causes of
F. Peptic ulcer disease and duodenal tumors were also considered among other causes of obstruction and were excluded by
G. Scleroderma and other collagen or vascular disorders were considered as mimics of the presentation

excluded_candidates: Gastrointestinal foreign body: no intrinsic luminal lesions on upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Gastric ulcer disease: no evidence of ulceration on endoscopy
Gastric malignancy: no evidence of mass on CT or endoscopy
